title: Pagan unwritten civil law does not prove unwritten faith-rules
source_text: XXVIII. Porro profanarum Rerumpublicarum exempla nihil moramur. Possunt illae quidem uti optime legibus non scriptis, in iis quae ad civilem gubernationem pertinent, quaeque adeo ab humanae rationis judicio pendent. At inde non sequitur parem esse rationem eorum quae pertinent ad fidem & cultum divinum. Cum enim ista habeantur ex divina revelatione, nec in iis quicquam ratio perspiciat, hominum curae atque memoriae non satis tuto committi potuerunt: ideoque divinae sapientiae consultum visum est, ut a viris divinitus inspiratis scripto mandarentur, quo facilius in Ecclesia possent incorrupta servari.
pass_a_gloss: Further, we care nothing for the examples of the profane Republics. They can indeed use unwritten laws very well in those things which pertain to civil government, and which therefore depend on the judgment of human reason. But it does not follow from that that there is equal reason in those things which pertain to faith and divine worship. For since these are had from divine revelation, and reason perceives nothing in them, they could not be committed safely enough to the care and memory of men: and therefore it seemed good to the counsel of divine wisdom that they be committed to writing by men divinely inspired, so that they could more easily be preserved uncorrupted in the Church.
pass_b_english: Athens and Sparta may run on unwritten civil custom — that lane is reason's.
Faith and worship come by revelation, not civic prudence.
Memory alone is not a safe vault for revealed things.
So wisdom had inspired men put them in writing for an uncorrupted church.

choices.term: inde non sequitur parem esse rationem eorum quae pertinent ad fidem
choices.english: it does not follow that there is equal reason in those things which pertain to faith
rejected: state custom proves church oral law
